Floor sums (类欧几里得): f(a, b, c, n) = Σi=0..n ⌊(a·i + b)/c⌋ in O(log) time. If a ≥ c or b ≥ c, pull out the whole parts: ⌊a/c⌋·n(n+1)/2 + ⌊b/c⌋·(n + 1) + f(a mod c, b mod c, c, n). Otherwise, with m = ⌊(a·n + b)/c⌋, count lattice points the other way: f = n·m − f(c, c − b − 1, a, m − 1). The parameters shrink like Euclid's algorithm.

A primitive root (原根) g modulo a prime p generates every non-zero residue: g, g², …, gp−1 are all different. Then every x ≠ 0 is gk for a unique k (its discrete log), which turns multiplication into addition (序列统计 in 拓展篇第8章 , and NTT's g = 3 for 998244353).

Test a candidate g: g is a primitive root iff g(p−1)/q ≠ 1 for every prime factor q of p − 1. Primitive roots are common (φ(p − 1) of them), so trying g = 2, 3, … finds the smallest quickly. Primitive roots exist exactly for 1, 2, 4, pᵏ and 2pᵏ (P6091 lists all of them).

Euler's criterion; Cipolla in u + vω.

A quadratic residue (二次剩余) modulo an odd prime p is n with x² ≡ n solvable. Euler's criterion: n(p−1)/2 ≡ 1 if it is a residue, −1 if not. Cipolla's algorithm finds x: pick random a with a² − n a non- residue (half of all a work), set ω² = a² − n, and compute (a + ω)(p+1)/2 in the field of numbers u + vω. The result has v = 0 and is a square root of n (P5491).
The two roots are x and p − x. Arithmetic in u + vω: (u₁ + v₁ω)(u₂ + v₂ω) = (u₁u₂ + v₁v₂ω²) + (u₁v₂ + u₂v₁)ω.

A = I + B/2 − 1; boundary by gcd.

Pick's theorem (皮克定理): for a polygon whose vertices are lattice points, area = I + B/2 − 1, where I is the number of lattice points strictly inside and B the number on the boundary. A segment from (x₁, y₁) to (x₂, y₂) contains gcd(|x₂ − x₁|, |y₂ − y₁|) + 1 lattice points, so B is a sum of gcds and I follows from the shoelace area.
Electric Fences (P2735): the triangle (0, 0), (n, m), (p, 0); count the lattice points strictly inside: I = A − B/2 + 1 with 2A = p·m.
Checked against testing every lattice point in the bounding box in Python. Each edge contributes gcd points without counting its starting vertex twice.
Working with 2A keeps everything an integer: I = (2A − B + 2) / 2.
U/R walk under a line; any monoid.

Universal Euclid (万能欧几里得): walk along the line y = (p·x + r) / q for x = 1..n and write "U" each time y passes an integer and "R" at each integer x. The string of U's and R's is built by a Euclid-like recursion in O(log) multiplications, if the quantity you want is a monoid: a node that knows how to combine two pieces of the walk.

类欧几里得(第 1 节) needs a new formula for every sum; universal Euclid needs only the merge rule. Below, a node stores (#R, #U, Σy, Σx·y) over its R steps; merging shifts the right part by the left part's counts. Matrices also form a monoid, which gives Σ Ax B⌊(px+r)/q⌋.

Key points to memorise
1. Floor sum: a ≥ c or b ≥ c ⇒ split off whole parts; else n·m − f(c, c−b−1, a, m−1).
2. Primitive root test: g^((p−1)/q) ≠ 1 for all prime q | p − 1.
3. Euler: n^((p−1)/2) = ±1 (residue / non-residue).
4. Cipolla: ω² = a² − n non-residue; (a + ω)^((p+1)/2).
5. Pick: A = I + B/2 − 1; segment points = gcd + 1.
6. Universal Euclid: U/R string of the line, built recursively with fast powers of monoid nodes.
